---
title: "Abstract Factory"
---

The **Abstract Factory** pattern provides an interface for creating *families of related objects* without specifying their concrete classes. Unlike Factory Method (which creates one product), Abstract Factory creates multiple products that belong together.

## Problem

Imagine you're building a game engine that supports different themes: Medieval and Sci-Fi. Each theme has its own units — warriors and buildings — that must match stylistically.

The naive approach uses conditionals to create themed objects, but this leads to:

- Repeated theme checks across multiple creation methods
- Risk of mixing incompatible products (Knight with Spaceship)
- Every new theme requires modifying existing code

### Example

```{mermaid}
flowchart TB
    GF[GameFactory]

    GF -->|"if medieval"| K[Knight]
    GF -->|"if scifi"| R[Robot]
    GF -->|"if medieval"| C[Castle]
    GF -->|"if scifi"| S[Spaceship]

    K -.-x S
    R -.-x C

    style GF fill:#f96,stroke:#333
    style K fill:#c9e,stroke:#333
    style C fill:#c9e,stroke:#333
    style R fill:#9ce,stroke:#333
    style S fill:#9ce,stroke:#333
```

**Problems with this approach:**

- Theme parameter must be passed to every creation method
- Nothing prevents mixing `Knight` with `Spaceship` (wrong family!)
- Adding a new theme requires modifying multiple methods

::: {.panel-tabset}
#### `Python`

```python
class Knight:
    def attack(self):
        print("Knight swings sword!")

class Robot:
    def attack(self):
        print("Robot fires laser!")

class Castle:
    def describe(self):
        print("A medieval stone castle")

class Spaceship:
    def describe(self):
        print("A futuristic spaceship base")

class GameFactory:
    def create_warrior(self, theme: str):
        if theme == "medieval":
            return Knight()
        elif theme == "scifi":
            return Robot()
        raise ValueError(f"Unknown theme: {theme}")

    def create_building(self, theme: str):
        if theme == "medieval":
            return Castle()
        elif theme == "scifi":
            return Spaceship()
        raise ValueError(f"Unknown theme: {theme}")
```

```csharp
public class Knight
{
    public void Attack() => Console.WriteLine("Knight swings sword!");
}

public class Robot
{
    public void Attack() => Console.WriteLine("Robot fires laser!");
}

public class Castle
{
    public void Describe() => Console.WriteLine("A medieval stone castle");
}

public class Spaceship
{
    public void Describe() => Console.WriteLine("A futuristic spaceship base");
}

public class GameFactory
{
    public object CreateWarrior(string theme) => theme switch
    {
        "medieval" => new Knight(),
        "scifi" => new Robot(),
        _ => throw new ArgumentException($"Unknown theme: {theme}")
    };

    public object CreateBuilding(string theme) => theme switch
    {
        "medieval" => new Castle(),
        "scifi" => new Spaceship(),
        _ => throw new ArgumentException($"Unknown theme: {theme}")
    };
}
```

#### `Dart`

```dart
class Knight {
  void attack() => print("Knight swings sword!");
}

class Robot {
  void attack() => print("Robot fires laser!");
}

class Castle {
  void describe() => print("A medieval stone castle");
}

class Spaceship {
  void describe() => print("A futuristic spaceship base");
}

class GameFactory {
  dynamic createWarrior(String theme) {
    switch (theme) {
      case "medieval": return Knight();
      case "scifi": return Robot();
      default: throw ArgumentError("Unknown theme: $theme");
    }
  }

  dynamic createBuilding(String theme) {
    switch (theme) {
      case "medieval": return Castle();
      case "scifi": return Spaceship();
      default: throw ArgumentError("Unknown theme: $theme");
    }
  }
}
```

#### `Rust`

```rust
// Rust needs one return type for "Knight or Robot", so each product kind
// becomes an enum, and every method still switches on the theme string
enum Warrior {
    Knight,
    Robot,
}

impl Warrior {
    fn attack(&self) {
        match self {
            Warrior::Knight => println!("Knight swings sword!"),
            Warrior::Robot => println!("Robot fires laser!"),
        }
    }
}

enum Building {
    Castle,
    Spaceship,
}

impl Building {
    fn describe(&self) {
        match self {
            Building::Castle => println!("A medieval stone castle"),
            Building::Spaceship => println!("A futuristic spaceship base"),
        }
    }
}

struct GameFactory;

impl GameFactory {
    fn create_warrior(&self, theme: &str) -> Warrior {
        match theme {
            "medieval" => Warrior::Knight,
            "scifi" => Warrior::Robot,
            _ => panic!("Unknown theme: {theme}"),
        }
    }

    fn create_building(&self, theme: &str) -> Building {
        match theme {
            "medieval" => Building::Castle,
            "scifi" => Building::Spaceship,
            _ => panic!("Unknown theme: {theme}"),
        }
    }
}
```

## Solution

The Abstract Factory pattern solves this by:

1. Defining **product interfaces** (`Warrior`, `Building`) for each product type
2. Creating an **abstract factory interface** (`GameFactory`) that declares creation methods for all products
3. Implementing **concrete factories** (`MedievalFactory`, `SciFiFactory`) that return matching product families

### UML Diagram

```{mermaid}
classDiagram
    class Warrior {
        <<interface>>
        +attack()
    }

    class Building {
        <<interface>>
        +describe()
    }

    class Knight {
        +attack()
    }

    class Robot {
        +attack()
    }

    class Castle {
        +describe()
    }

    class Spaceship {
        +describe()
    }

    class GameFactory {
        <<interface>>
        +createWarrior() Warrior
        +createBuilding() Building
    }

    class MedievalFactory {
        +createWarrior() Warrior
        +createBuilding() Building
    }

    class SciFiFactory {
        +createWarrior() Warrior
        +createBuilding() Building
    }

    Warrior <|.. Knight
    Warrior <|.. Robot
    Building <|.. Castle
    Building <|.. Spaceship

    GameFactory <|.. MedievalFactory
    GameFactory <|.. SciFiFactory

    MedievalFactory ..> Knight : creates
    MedievalFactory ..> Castle : creates
    SciFiFactory ..> Robot : creates
    SciFiFactory ..> Spaceship : creates
```

### Refactored Code

::: {.panel-tabset}
#### `Python`

```python
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

# Product interfaces
class Warrior(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def attack(self) -> None:
        pass

class Building(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def describe(self) -> None:
        pass

# Concrete Products - Medieval
class Knight(Warrior):
    def attack(self) -> None:
        print("Knight swings sword!")

class Castle(Building):
    def describe(self) -> None:
        print("A medieval stone castle")

# Concrete Products - Sci-Fi
class Robot(Warrior):
    def attack(self) -> None:
        print("Robot fires laser!")

class Spaceship(Building):
    def describe(self) -> None:
        print("A futuristic spaceship base")

# Abstract Factory
class GameFactory(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def create_warrior(self) -> Warrior:
        pass

    @abstractmethod
    def create_building(self) -> Building:
        pass

# Concrete Factories
class MedievalFactory(GameFactory):
    def create_warrior(self) -> Warrior:
        return Knight()

    def create_building(self) -> Building:
        return Castle()

class SciFiFactory(GameFactory):
    def create_warrior(self) -> Warrior:
        return Robot()

    def create_building(self) -> Building:
        return Spaceship()
```

```dart
// Product interfaces
abstract class Warrior {
  void attack();
}

abstract class Building {
  void describe();
}

// Concrete Products - Medieval
class Knight implements Warrior {

  void attack() => print("Knight swings sword!");

class Castle implements Building {

// Concrete Products - Sci-Fi

  @override
  void attack() => print("Robot fires laser!");
}

class Spaceship implements Building {
  @override
  void describe() => print("A futuristic spaceship base");
}

// Abstract Factory
abstract class GameFactory {
  Warrior createWarrior();
  Building createBuilding();
}

// Concrete Factories

  Warrior createWarrior() => Knight();

  @override
```

#### `Rust`

```rust
// Product interfaces → traits
trait Warrior {
    fn attack(&self);
}

trait Building {
    fn describe(&self);
}

// Concrete Products - Medieval
struct Knight;

impl Warrior for Knight {
    fn attack(&self) {
        println!("Knight swings sword!");
    }
}

struct Castle;

impl Building for Castle {
    fn describe(&self) {
        println!("A medieval stone castle");
    }
}

// Concrete Products - Sci-Fi
struct Robot;

impl Warrior for Robot {
    fn attack(&self) {
        println!("Robot fires laser!");
    }
}

struct Spaceship;

impl Building for Spaceship {
    fn describe(&self) {
        println!("A futuristic spaceship base");
    }
}

// Abstract Factory → a trait with one creation method per product
trait GameFactory {
    fn create_warrior(&self) -> Box<dyn Warrior>;
    fn create_building(&self) -> Box<dyn Building>;
}

// Concrete Factories → unit structs, one per family
struct MedievalFactory;

impl GameFactory for MedievalFactory {
    fn create_warrior(&self) -> Box<dyn Warrior> {
        Box::new(Knight)
    }

    fn create_building(&self) -> Box<dyn Building> {
        Box::new(Castle)
    }
}

struct SciFiFactory;

impl GameFactory for SciFiFactory {
    fn create_warrior(&self) -> Box<dyn Warrior> {
        Box::new(Robot)
    }

    fn create_building(&self) -> Box<dyn Building> {
        Box::new(Spaceship)
    }
}
```

:::

```python
def play_game(factory: GameFactory) -> None:
    warrior = factory.create_warrior()
    building = factory.create_building()

    warrior.attack()
    building.describe()

# Products are guaranteed to match!
play_game(MedievalFactory())  # Knight + Castle
play_game(SciFiFactory())     # Robot + Spaceship
```

:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="🦀 Rust lens"}
| GoF role | Rust |
|---|---|
| Product interfaces | `trait Warrior`, `trait Building` |
| Concrete products | unit structs `Knight`, `Castle`, `Robot`, `Spaceship` |
| Abstract factory | `trait GameFactory` with one `create_*` method per product |
| Concrete factory | `struct MedievalFactory` + `impl GameFactory for MedievalFactory` |
| Client's factory reference | `&dyn GameFactory` |

**Ownership:** each `create_*` method returns a `Box<dyn …>`, so the client owns products whose concrete types it never names. The factories are unit structs with no fields, so passing `&MedievalFactory` costs nothing. The Problem code shows the other side: without traits, "Knight or Robot" needs an enum per product kind, and nothing ties the two enums to one theme. See the [OOP Cheatsheet](../oop/oop-cheatsheet.qmd#rust) for the general mapping.
:::

## Modern Approach

Each concrete factory above is a class whose methods only call constructors. A product family is really just *a fixed set of constructors that belong together*. All five languages can hold that set in one small immutable value, such as a record, an object literal, or a Rust struct of `fn` pointers. Each theme then becomes a one-line preset instead of a class. Rust can also tie a family together at the type level with associated types, shown after the code.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Verdict: 🟡 Simplifies** — a factory family becomes a record of constructors, so the factory classes disappear. The product interfaces stay.
:::

### Feature Map

::: {.panel-tabset}
#### `Python`

| Classic | Modern |
|---|---|
| `class GameFactory(ABC)` with abstract `create_warrior()` / `create_building()` | `@dataclass(frozen=True) class GameFactory` with two callable fields |
| `class MedievalFactory(GameFactory)` | preset `MEDIEVAL = GameFactory(create_warrior=Knight, create_building=Castle)` |
| `def create_warrior(self): return Knight()` | `Knight` itself: a class is already a no-arg factory |
| `Warrior`, `Building`, and the four products | unchanged |

#### `C#`

| Classic | Modern |
|---|---|
| `interface IGameFactory` with `CreateWarrior()` / `CreateBuilding()` | `record GameFactory(Func<IWarrior> CreateWarrior, Func<IBuilding> CreateBuilding)` |
| `class MedievalFactory : IGameFactory` | preset `Themes.Medieval = new(() => new Knight(), () => new Castle())` |
| Calling `factory.CreateWarrior()` | unchanged: a delegate property is invoked like a method |
| `IWarrior`, `IBuilding`, and the four products | unchanged |

#### `TypeScript`

| Classic | Modern |
|---|---|
| `interface GameFactory` with `createWarrior()` / `createBuilding()` | unchanged |
| `class MedievalFactory implements GameFactory` | `const medieval = { createWarrior: …, createBuilding: … } satisfies GameFactory` |
| `new MedievalFactory()` | `medieval`: a plain object, no instantiation |
| `Warrior`, `Building`, and the four products | unchanged |

#### `Dart`

| Classic | Modern |
|---|---|
| `abstract class GameFactory` with `createWarrior()` / `createBuilding()` | `typedef GameFactory = ({Warrior Function() createWarrior, Building Function() createBuilding})` |
| `class MedievalFactory implements GameFactory` | `const medieval = (createWarrior: Knight.new, createBuilding: Castle.new)` |
| `Warrior createWarrior() => Knight();` | `Knight.new`: a constructor tear-off |
| `Warrior`, `Building`, and the four products | unchanged |

#### `Rust`

| Classic | Modern |
|---|---|
| `trait GameFactory` with `create_warrior()` / `create_building()` | `struct GameFactory` with two `fn() -> Box<dyn …>` fields |
| `struct MedievalFactory` + `impl GameFactory for MedievalFactory` | preset `const MEDIEVAL: GameFactory = GameFactory { … }` |
| `fn create_warrior(&self) -> Box<dyn Warrior> { Box::new(Knight) }` | a closure that captures nothing, coerced to a `fn` pointer |
| `&dyn GameFactory` | `&GameFactory`: a plain struct, so the factory itself needs no vtable |
| `Warrior`, `Building`, and the four products | unchanged |

:::

**Ecosystem:** DI containers swap a whole family at the composition root, for example by registering a different set of implementations per environment or theme. Flutter's `ThemeData` applies the same idea to styling: one value that bundles matching colors, fonts, and widget themes.

### Modern Code

::: {.panel-tabset}
#### `Python`

```python
# Python 3.10+ — frozen dataclass of callables; classes are callables
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod
from collections.abc import Callable
from dataclasses import dataclass


# Products → unchanged
class Warrior(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def attack(self) -> None: ...


class Building(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def describe(self) -> None: ...


class Knight(Warrior):
    def attack(self) -> None:
        print("Knight swings sword!")


class Castle(Building):
    def describe(self) -> None:
        print("A medieval stone castle")


class Robot(Warrior):
    def attack(self) -> None:
        print("Robot fires laser!")


class Spaceship(Building):
    def describe(self) -> None:
        print("A futuristic spaceship base")


# Abstract factory → a record of constructors
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class GameFactory:
    create_warrior: Callable[[], Warrior]
    create_building: Callable[[], Building]


# Concrete factories → presets (a class is already a factory)
MEDIEVAL = GameFactory(create_warrior=Knight, create_building=Castle)
SCI_FI = GameFactory(create_warrior=Robot, create_building=Spaceship)


def play_game(factory: GameFactory) -> None:
    warrior = factory.create_warrior()
    building = factory.create_building()

    warrior.attack()
    building.describe()


# --- Usage ---
# Products are still guaranteed to match: each preset is one family
play_game(MEDIEVAL)  # Knight swings sword! / A medieval stone castle
play_game(SCI_FI)  # Robot fires laser! / A futuristic spaceship base
```

#### `C#`

```csharp
// C# 10+ / .NET 8+ — positional record of Func<> delegates

// Products → unchanged
public interface IWarrior
{
    void Attack();
}

public interface IBuilding
{
    void Describe();
}

public class Knight : IWarrior
{
    public void Attack() => Console.WriteLine("Knight swings sword!");
}

public class Castle : IBuilding
{
    public void Describe() => Console.WriteLine("A medieval stone castle");
}

public class Robot : IWarrior
{
    public void Attack() => Console.WriteLine("Robot fires laser!");
}

public class Spaceship : IBuilding
{
    public void Describe() => Console.WriteLine("A futuristic spaceship base");
}

// Abstract factory → a record of constructors
public record GameFactory(Func<IWarrior> CreateWarrior, Func<IBuilding> CreateBuilding);

// Concrete factories → presets
public static class Themes
{
    public static readonly GameFactory Medieval = new(() => new Knight(), () => new Castle());
    public static readonly GameFactory SciFi = new(() => new Robot(), () => new Spaceship());
}

// --- Usage ---
void PlayGame(GameFactory factory)
{
    var warrior = factory.CreateWarrior();  // a delegate property is called like a method
    var building = factory.CreateBuilding();

    warrior.Attack();
    building.Describe();
}

// Products are still guaranteed to match: each preset is one family
PlayGame(Themes.Medieval);  // Knight swings sword! / A medieval stone castle
PlayGame(Themes.SciFi);     // Robot fires laser! / A futuristic spaceship base
```

```typescript
// TypeScript 4.9+ — object literals checked with `satisfies`

// Products → unchanged
interface Warrior {
  attack(): void;
}

interface Building {
  describe(): void;
}

class Knight implements Warrior {
  attack(): void {
    console.log("Knight swings sword!");
  }
}

class Castle implements Building {
  describe(): void {
    console.log("A medieval stone castle");

class Robot implements Warrior {
  attack(): void {
    console.log("Robot fires laser!");
  }
}

class Spaceship implements Building {
  describe(): void {
    console.log("A futuristic spaceship base");
  }
}

// Abstract factory → unchanged interface
interface GameFactory {
  createWarrior(): Warrior;
  createBuilding(): Building;
}

// Concrete factories → object literals instead of classes
const medieval = {
  createWarrior: () => new Knight(),
  createBuilding: () => new Castle(),
} satisfies GameFactory;

const sciFi = {
  createWarrior: () => new Robot(),
  createBuilding: () => new Spaceship(),
} satisfies GameFactory;

function playGame(factory: GameFactory): void {
  const warrior = factory.createWarrior();
  const building = factory.createBuilding();

  warrior.attack();
  building.describe();
}

// --- Usage ---
// Products are still guaranteed to match: each preset is one family
playGame(medieval);  // Knight swings sword! / A medieval stone castle
playGame(sciFi);     // Robot fires laser! / A futuristic spaceship base
```

#### `Dart`

```dart
// Dart 3.x — records of constructor tear-offs

// Products → unchanged
abstract class Warrior {
  void attack();
}

abstract class Building {
  void describe();
}

class Knight implements Warrior {
  @override
  void attack() => print("Knight swings sword!");
}

class Castle implements Building {
  @override
  void describe() => print("A medieval stone castle");
}

class Robot implements Warrior {
  @override
  void attack() => print("Robot fires laser!");
}

class Spaceship implements Building {
  @override
  void describe() => print("A futuristic spaceship base");
}

// Abstract factory → a record type of constructors
typedef GameFactory = ({
  Warrior Function() createWarrior,
  Building Function() createBuilding,
});

// Concrete factories → const presets of constructor tear-offs
const GameFactory medieval = (createWarrior: Knight.new, createBuilding: Castle.new);
const GameFactory sciFi = (createWarrior: Robot.new, createBuilding: Spaceship.new);

void playGame(GameFactory factory) {
  final warrior = factory.createWarrior();
  final building = factory.createBuilding();

  warrior.attack();
  building.describe();
}

// --- Usage ---
void main() {
  // Products are still guaranteed to match: each preset is one family
  playGame(medieval);  // Knight swings sword! / A medieval stone castle
  playGame(sciFi);     // Robot fires laser! / A futuristic spaceship base
}
```

#### `Rust`

```rust
// Rust 1.85+ (edition 2024) — struct of fn pointers, const presets
// Products → unchanged
trait Warrior {
    fn attack(&self);
}

trait Building {
    fn describe(&self);
}

struct Knight;

impl Warrior for Knight {
    fn attack(&self) {
        println!("Knight swings sword!");
    }
}

struct Castle;

impl Building for Castle {
    fn describe(&self) {
        println!("A medieval stone castle");
    }
}

struct Robot;

impl Warrior for Robot {
    fn attack(&self) {
        println!("Robot fires laser!");
    }
}

struct Spaceship;

impl Building for Spaceship {
    fn describe(&self) {
        println!("A futuristic spaceship base");
    }
}

// Abstract factory → a record of constructors
struct GameFactory {
    create_warrior: fn() -> Box<dyn Warrior>,
    create_building: fn() -> Box<dyn Building>,
}

// Concrete factories → presets (a closure that captures nothing is a `fn` pointer)
const MEDIEVAL: GameFactory = GameFactory {
    create_warrior: || Box::new(Knight),
    create_building: || Box::new(Castle),
};

const SCI_FI: GameFactory = GameFactory {
    create_warrior: || Box::new(Robot),
    create_building: || Box::new(Spaceship),
};

fn play_game(factory: &GameFactory) {
    let warrior = (factory.create_warrior)();
    let building = (factory.create_building)();
    warrior.attack();
    building.describe();
}

// --- Usage ---
fn main() {
    // Products are still guaranteed to match: each preset is one family
    play_game(&MEDIEVAL); // Knight swings sword! / A medieval stone castle
    play_game(&SCI_FI); // Robot fires laser! / A futuristic spaceship base
}
```

:::

#### Rust: Families as Associated Types

When the theme is known at compile time, a Rust trait can name each family's product types. `Medieval::Warrior` *is* `Knight`, so the products need no `Box` and every call is dispatched statically. A signature such as `defend<T: Theme>(warrior: T::Warrior, building: T::Building)` accepts only a matching pair.

```rust
// Rust 1.85+ — associated types: each family names its own product types
trait Warrior {
    fn attack(&self);
}

trait Building {
    fn describe(&self);
}

struct Knight;

impl Warrior for Knight {
    fn attack(&self) {
        println!("Knight swings sword!");
    }
}

struct Castle;

impl Building for Castle {
    fn describe(&self) {
        println!("A medieval stone castle");
    }
}

struct Robot;

impl Warrior for Robot {
    fn attack(&self) {
        println!("Robot fires laser!");
    }
}

struct Spaceship;

impl Building for Spaceship {
    fn describe(&self) {
        println!("A futuristic spaceship base");
    }
}

// A theme is a type; its products are associated types of that theme
trait Theme {
    type Warrior: Warrior;
    type Building: Building;
    fn create_warrior() -> Self::Warrior;
    fn create_building() -> Self::Building;
}

struct Medieval;

impl Theme for Medieval {
    type Warrior = Knight;
    type Building = Castle;

    fn create_warrior() -> Knight {
        Knight
    }

    fn create_building() -> Castle {
        Castle
    }
}

struct SciFi;

impl Theme for SciFi {
    type Warrior = Robot;
    type Building = Spaceship;

    fn create_warrior() -> Robot {
        Robot
    }

    fn create_building() -> Spaceship {
        Spaceship
    }
}

// Static dispatch: one compiled copy per theme, no Box, no vtable
fn play_game<T: Theme>() {
    T::create_warrior().attack();
    T::create_building().describe();
}

// A family-typed signature: only a matching pair compiles
fn defend<T: Theme>(warrior: T::Warrior, building: T::Building) {
    warrior.attack();
    building.describe();
}

fn main() {
    play_game::<Medieval>(); // Knight swings sword! / A medieval stone castle
    play_game::<SciFi>(); // Robot fires laser! / A futuristic spaceship base
    defend::<Medieval>(Knight, Castle); // Knight swings sword! / A medieval stone castle
    // defend::<Medieval>(Knight, Spaceship); // ❌ error[E0308]: mismatched types
}
```

### Classic or Modern?

| Prefer a record of constructors when | Keep factory classes when |
|---|---|
| Each factory method only calls a constructor | Creating a product needs logic or dependencies (config, connections) per family |
| Families are a small, known set of presets | Families are plug-ins loaded at runtime and need a named type |
| A new theme should be a one-line addition | The factory keeps shared state across the products it creates (a seed, a cache, an ID counter) |
| Rust: the theme is picked at runtime, so a `&GameFactory` preset is enough | Rust: the theme is fixed at compile time and products should skip the `Box` (associated types, above) |

## Summary

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" collapse="false"}
**Abstract Factory** ensures that products created together are compatible, preventing mismatched combinations and making it easy to swap entire product families.
:::

### Key Benefits

- **Product Consistency**: Factory guarantees all products belong to the same family
- **Open/Closed Principle**: Add new themes by creating new factory classes — no existing code changes
- **Single Responsibility**: Each factory is responsible for one product family
- **Loose Coupling**: Client code depends only on abstract interfaces

### When to Use

| ✅ Use When | ❌ Avoid When |
|------------|--------------|
| Products come in families that must be used together | You only have one product type (use Factory Method) |
| You need to enforce consistency across related products | Product families rarely change |
| System should be independent of how products are created | The additional abstraction adds unnecessary complexity |
| You want to swap entire product families easily | |
